yarn-troppo.meaning: Every beat is there: the uncertain date, the flume, betting either side, the list of fights, the straddle-bug to Mexico, the parson's wife ("Well, I'll risk two-and-a-half she don't, anyway."), and the mare. Additions such as "To the parson's face! True story." and "Every time!" react to what is there and invent nothing.
yarn-troppo.sense: Terms fit: "lobbed at the camp" for arriving, "cashed up or flat broke" for flush or busted, "crook as a dog" for very sick, "some such lurgy" for the mare's ailments, "takin' the piss" for "only in fun". "the best fire-and-brimstone man" stretches "exhorter" a little but holds.
yarn-troppo.authenticity: Mostly sounds like a real Aussie yarn-spinner: "luckier than a shithouse rat", "Didn't matter a skerrick to him", "I'm blowed if I can remember now". A few stock pieces: "no worries", "happy as Larry", and the rhyming slang "on the frog and toad", which is more stage than speech.
yarn-troppo.register: Full level-5 yarn with swearing inside the vulgarity-2 limit: "luckier than a shithouse rat", "takin' the piss", "every bloody time", "wherever the hell he was headed".
yarn-troppo.tone: Keeps the narrator's garrulous, oblivious drawl, but asides like "Now get this." and "To the parson's face! True story." nudge the reader to the joke, where Twain's narrator tells it deadpan.
yarn-troppo.flow: Reads aloud easily; the list is punched up well ("Horse race? You'd find him cashed up or flat broke at the end of it. Dog fight? He'd bet on it.") and the long mare sentence keeps its run.
yarn-troppo.variety: Varied slang throughout: "cove", "poor mug", "bloke", "skerrick", "lurgy", "the folding stuff", "het up"; no tic repeats.
yarn-troppo.essence: Unmistakably the Smiley monologue: the rambling dialect ("solit'ry", "foller", "Prov'dence", "the dangdest feller") and the shape of the yarn are kept.

engine.meaning: Most of the original is left as is, but some lines change: "and a dead-set legend, mate" replaces "and a good man", "before he reckoned" garbles "before he thought", and "the young fellas" for "the boys".
engine.sense: Several terms take the wrong sense: "she get rapt'n desperate like" (rapt is delighted, not excited), "before he reckoned" (reckon is to think-as-opinion, not to stop and think), "ya flamin' mongrel" aimed at nobody, "a dead-set legend" for a good parson.
engine.authenticity: Stage-Australian tags bolted onto the untranslated original: "Crikey, he was always ready", "Jeez, if he even see", "cobber. Stone the flamin' crows."
engine.register: Swearing stays within vulgarity 2 ("for a fuckin' good while", "lucky bugger"), and there is a lot of slang, but it is tags on Twain's text rather than an Aussie retelling, so the weight sits only in patches.
engine.tone: The tone wobbles: "for a fuckin' good while" about the parson's dying wife and the insult "ya flamin' mongrel" jar with the narrator's genial, innocent manner.
engine.flow: Clunky joins: "Anyway, why, it never made no difference", "bloody big flume", "dust'n raisin'", and a tagged-on ending "cobber. Stone the flamin' crows."
engine.variety: Lots of different tags ("Crikey", "Jeez", "Fair dinkum", "mate", "cobber") but they are interjections of one kind, a few of them leaned on: "flamin'" twice, "bloody" twice.
engine.essence: Recognisably the original, since most of Twain's text is untouched ("the curiousest cove about always betting on anythin' that lobbed ya ever see"), but the inserted tags blur the narrator's character.

yarn-dinkum.meaning: Every point is kept, from "the big flume wasn't finished" to "I'll risk two-and-a-half she don't, anyway." and the mare "just about a neck in front".
yarn-dinkum.sense: Terms fit: "rolled up to the camp", "cashed up or ... stony broke", "bloody crook", "she'd come good yet", "win the foldin' stuff".
yarn-dinkum.authenticity: Natural throughout: "it never made a skerrick of difference to him", "pickin' up that quick", "slow as a funeral"; only "the frog and toad" reads as stock.
yarn-dinkum.register: Plenty of Aussie, but the swearing stops at vulgarity 1 ("lucky bugger", "bloody crook") and the retelling keeps close to Twain's lines, so a touch lighter than a level-5, vulgarity-2 pub yarn.
yarn-dinkum.tone: The deadpan, rambling earnestness holds; the punchline comes "without thinkin'" and is left to land on its own.
yarn-dinkum.flow: Smooth and conversational: "and if ya took him on, he'd foller that straddle-bug all the way to Mexico to find out where he was bound for".
yarn-dinkum.variety: Good spread: "cove", "bloke", "chook fight", "strewth", "skerrick", "het up"; "ya" is frequent but natural.
yarn-dinkum.essence: Keeps the dialect markers ("solit'ry", "foller", "Prov'dence", "the dangdest feller") and the run-on shape; unmistakably Smiley.

dinkum-3.meaning: All the facts survive ("the big flume wasn't finished", the fights, the straddle-bug, the parson's wife, the mare).
dinkum-3.sense: Terms fit: "lobbed at the camp", "cashed up or stony broke", "bloody crook", "comin' good so quick".
dinkum-3.authenticity: Natural Aussie ("lucky as", "happy as Larry", "some bugger to take the other side"), with the stock "frog and toad".
dinkum-3.register: Swearing stops at vulgarity 1 ("bloody crook", "lucky bugger") and the slang is moderate; a bit light for level 5, vulgarity 2.
dinkum-3.tone: Keeps the deadpan rambling and lets the punchline land plain: "Smiley, without even thinkin', goes".
dinkum-3.flow: Reads smoothly: "dog fight, he'd bet on it; cat fight, he'd bet on it; chook fight, he'd bet on it".
dinkum-3.variety: Leans on "bloke": "the strangest bloke", "the other bloke", "a good bloke with it", "strangest bloke goin'", "the blokes".
dinkum-3.essence: Recognisable, but Twain's dialect is normalised: "the dangdest feller" becomes "strangest bloke goin'", "she don't" becomes "she doesn't", "inf'nite" becomes "endless", "Prov'dence" becomes "Providence".

unharnessed.meaning: All the points survive, the punchline made explicit: "'Well, I'll put two and a half on her not making it, anyway.'"
unharnessed.sense: Terms fit: "rocked up at the camp", "have a punt on it", "rolling in it or flat stony broke", "crook, real crook".
unharnessed.authenticity: Mostly natural modern Aussie ("some other poor sod", "have a punt on it", "the mad bastard"), but "lucky as all get-out" is an American idiom.
unharnessed.register: Level 5 with swearing at vulgarity 2: "the lucky bastard", "the arse end of the race", "taking the piss", "some bloody thing".
unharnessed.tone: Keeps the joke and the narrator's admiration, but the clipped modern sentences ("Nearly always came out on top.") trade the oblivious drawl for punchier banter.
unharnessed.flow: Reads easily aloud; short sentences, clean joins: "Cat fight, he'd bet on it. Chook fight, he'd bet on it."
unharnessed.variety: Varied, though "bloody" recurs: "any bloody thing", "Made no bloody difference", "some bloody thing", "every bloody time".
unharnessed.essence: The story is intact, but Twain's dialect ("solit'ry", "foller", "dangdest", "warn't") is stripped and the breathless run-on monologue chopped into short modern sentences, flattening what makes it itself.

yarn-troppo.quote: To the parson's face! True story.
yarn-troppo.why: Added aside spells out the joke; Twain's narrator never notices it is funny.
Cockney rhyming slang reads as stock Aussie pastiche; rarely heard in speech.

yarn-troppo.original: and if he couldn't he'd change sides
yarn-troppo.why: Stock phrase bolted onto the line.

engine.original: and if he couldn't he'd change sides
engine.why: An insult addressed to no one; changes the friendly narrator into an abusive one.
Wrong register for praising a preacher; changes 'good man' into a youth-slang compliment.
Swearing about the parson's wife's illness; an Australian would wince at it here.
Reckon means to suppose; the sense of acting before thinking is lost.

engine.original: she get excited and desperate like
engine.why: Rapt means delighted, not excited; wrong sense.
Shifts 'the boys' (the camp men) to young men.
Stock stage-Australian tags bolted on at the end.
Swear dropped in where it adds nothing.

yarn-dinkum.quote: how long he was on the frog and toad
yarn-dinkum.original: how long he was on the road
yarn-dinkum.why: Rhyming slang reads as stock pastiche.
Swearing stays light for a vulgarity-2 brief; fine, but under the weight asked.

dinkum-3.why: Loses the signature dialect word and repeats 'strangest bloke' from earlier.
Standardises the narrator's grammar, flattening the dialect in the punchline.

dinkum-3.original: thank the Lord for his inf'nite mercy
dinkum-3.why: Needless change to a fixed pious phrase.

unharnessed.why: Clipped, standardised grammar drops the narrator's dialect; representative of the whole text.

summaries.yarn-troppo: A rich, natural level-5 retelling that keeps Twain's dialect and every detail; a couple of nudging asides and stock phrases are its only weak spots.
summaries.engine: Twain's text with Aussie tags pasted in; several land in the wrong sense or place, and the tone jars.
summaries.yarn-dinkum: A faithful, natural retelling that keeps Twain's voice; slightly light on the vulgarity the brief allows.
summaries.dinkum-3: Clean and faithful with natural Aussie, but plainer than the brief and it irons out Twain's dialect.
summaries.unharnessed: Fluent, properly vulgar modern Aussie retelling with every point kept, but it strips Twain's dialect and run-on shape, and slips in an Americanism.
